questions.q: What characterises the bottom-up approach to implementing information security?
o: It is initiated by upper management who issue policies and dictate goals
It begins as a grassroots effort in which systems administrators try to improve the security of their own systems
It relies entirely on off-the-shelf software
It requires a formal systems development life cycle
questions.e: The bottom-up approach is a grassroots effort in which systems administrators attempt to improve the security of their systems, drawing on their in-depth technical knowledge of the threats and mechanisms involved.

questions.q: Why does the bottom-up approach to information security seldom succeed?
o: Administrators lack technical expertise
It lacks critical features such as participant support and organizational staying power
It is initiated by upper management
It costs too much money
questions.e: Although the bottom-up approach benefits from administrators' technical expertise, it seldom works because it lacks critical features such as participant support and organizational staying power.

questions.q: Which approach to information security implementation has a higher probability of success, and why?
o: Bottom-up, because administrators know the threats best
Top-down, because it has strong upper-management support, a dedicated champion, dedicated funding, and a clear planning process
Neither; both have equal success rates
The grassroots approach, because it is cheaper
questions.e: The top-down approach has a higher probability of success because it is initiated by upper management and has strong upper-management support, a dedicated champion, usually dedicated funding, a clear planning and implementation process, and the means of influencing organizational culture.

questions.q: What formal development strategy does the most successful kind of top-down approach involve?
o: Agile development
A systems development life cycle (SDLC)
Rapid application development
Bottom-up prototyping
questions.e: The most successful top-down approach also involves a formal development strategy known as a systems development life cycle (SDLC).

questions.q: What is the systems development life cycle (SDLC)?
o: A method for encrypting data
A methodology for the design and implementation of an information system
A type of firewall configuration
A hashing algorithm
questions.e: The SDLC is a methodology for the design and implementation of an information system; its phases generally address the investigation, analysis, design, implementation, and maintenance of an information system.

questions.q: The general phases of the traditional (waterfall) SDLC address which activities?
o: Encryption, decryption, hashing, signing, and verifying
Investigation, analysis, design, implementation, and maintenance
Bottom-up, top-down, grassroots, and executive
Confidentiality, integrity, availability, and authenticity
questions.e: The SDLC's phases generally address the investigation, analysis, design, implementation, and maintenance of an information system.

questions.q: What is software assurance (SA)?
o: A warranty offered by software vendors
A methodological approach to software development that seeks to build security into the development life cycle rather than address it at later stages
A type of antivirus software
A licensing agreement
questions.e: Software assurance (SA) is a methodological approach to software development that builds security into the development life cycle rather than addressing it later; it intentionally creates software free of vulnerabilities that can be deployed with confidence.

questions.q: The U.S. Department of Defense launched a Software Assurance Initiative in which year, and what did it produce?
o: 1998; the ISO 27000 series
2003; the Secure Software Assurance (SwA) Common Body of Knowledge (CBK)
2010; the NIST Cybersecurity Framework
2016; the GDPR
questions.e: The U.S. Department of Defense launched a Software Assurance Initiative in 2003 (led by Joe Jarzombek, endorsed by the Department of Homeland Security in 2004), which resulted in the Secure Software Assurance (SwA) Common Body of Knowledge (CBK).

questions.q: How many phases does the simplified NIST SDLC use?
o: Three
Four
Five
Seven
questions.e: NIST adopted a simplified SDLC based on five phases: Initiation, Development/Acquisition, Implementation/Assessment, Operation/Maintenance, and Disposal.

questions.q: Which set correctly lists the five phases of the NIST SDLC in order?
o: Investigation, Analysis, Design, Implementation, Maintenance
Initiation, Development/Acquisition, Implementation/Assessment, Operation/Maintenance, Disposal
Plan, Do, Check, Act, Review
Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover
questions.e: The NIST SDLC's five phases are Initiation, Development/Acquisition, Implementation/Assessment, Operation/Maintenance, and Disposal.

questions.q: In the NIST approach to securing the SDLC, who is responsible for ensuring the secure use of commercial off-the-shelf software (COTS)?
o: The software vendor alone
The implementing organization
The NIST agency
No one is responsible for COTS
questions.e: Whether a system is custom-made, built from scratch, customized, or purchased commercial off-the-shelf software (COTS), the implementing organization is responsible for ensuring its secure use.

questions.q: According to the NIST approach, what must each system implementation avoid compromising?
o: The speed and usability of the system
The confidentiality, integrity, and availability of the organization's information assets
The organization's marketing strategy
The vendor's licensing terms
questions.e: Each implementation of a system should be secure and should not risk compromising the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of the organization's information assets.

questions.q: Why is software assurance important to overall system security?
o: Because hardware never fails
Because many information security issues have their root cause in the software elements of the system, so secure systems require secure or at least securable software
Because software cannot be encrypted
Because software assurance replaces the need for the SDLC
questions.e: Many of the information security issues facing modern information systems have their root cause in the software elements of the system; secure systems require secure or at least securable software.

questions.q: The Secure Software Assurance Common Body of Knowledge (SwA CBK) is best described as what?
o: A legally binding government standard
A strongly recommended guide for developing more secure applications (not yet adopted as a standard or policy requirement)
A commercial antivirus product
An encryption algorithm
questions.e: Although the SwA CBK has not yet been adopted as a standard or even a policy requirement of government agencies, it serves as a strongly recommended guide to developing more secure applications.

questions.q: Securing an organization's information assets is described as what kind of process?
o: An instantaneous, one-time event
An incremental process that requires coordination, time, and patience
A purely automated process needing no human effort
A process that can happen overnight
questions.e: Securing information assets is an incremental process that requires coordination, time, and patience; it must begin somewhere and cannot happen overnight.

questions.q: The Caesar cipher encrypts a message by doing what?
o: Rearranging the positions of the letters
Shifting each letter of the alphabet by a fixed amount (for example, by 3)
Replacing words with page and line numbers
Hashing the message into a fixed-length digest
questions.e: The Caesar cipher is a substitution cipher that shifts letters by a fixed amount (classically by 3), so each plaintext letter is replaced by the letter a fixed number of positions later in the alphabet.

questions.q: In the Vigenère cipher, how is a ciphertext letter determined for a given plaintext and keyword letter?
o: By shifting the plaintext letter by 3 positions
By finding the row for the keyword letter and the column for the plaintext letter; their intersection is the ciphertext letter
By looking up the plaintext letter's page and line number
By XORing the two letters
questions.e: Using the Vigenère table (tabula recta), you find the row for the keyword letter and the column for the plaintext letter; the letter at their intersection is the ciphertext letter.

questions.q: In a transposition cipher, what happens to the letters of the message?
o: The letters are substituted with other letters
The letters are not changed, but their positions are rearranged according to a specific pattern or key
The letters are converted to numbers
The letters are hashed
questions.e: A transposition cipher does not change the letters of the message; instead, it rearranges their positions according to a specific pattern or key.

questions.q: What does a book cipher use as its key, and what does the ciphertext consist of?
o: A secret number; the ciphertext is a shifted alphabet
A book; the ciphertext consists of page, line, and word numbers, and both sender and receiver must have the same book
A password; the ciphertext is a hash
A one-time pad; the ciphertext is random noise
questions.e: A book cipher uses a book as the key; the ciphertext consists of page, line, and word numbers, and both sender and receiver must have the same book (dictionaries and thesauruses are popular choices).

questions.q: How does a running key cipher differ from the Vigenère cipher when the key needs to be extended?
o: It repeats the key from the beginning
Instead of repeating the key, it continues the text from the indicator block (the predetermined book)
It switches to a Caesar shift
It stops encrypting
questions.e: The running key cipher uses a book to pass the key, similar to Vigenère; but unlike Vigenère, if the key needs to be extended you do not repeat the key — you continue the text from the indicator block.

questions.q: The template (perforated page) cipher is best classified as an example of what?
o: Symmetric encryption
Steganography (hiding a message)
A hash function
Asymmetric encryption
questions.e: The template or perforated page cipher is not strictly an encryption cipher but an example of steganography: the receiver places a page with holes over the text to reveal a hidden message.

questions.q: A simpler alternative to the template cipher, in which the first letter of each line (or every nth letter) spells a hidden message, is called what?
o: A book cipher
A variation of acrostics
A transposition cipher
A running key cipher
questions.e: A much simpler steganographic method than the perforated-page template is a variation of acrostics, where the first letter of each line of a message (or every nth letter) spells out the hidden message.

questions.q: A drawback of the template (perforated page) cipher is which of the following?
o: It requires a computer to execute
It is easy to detect: the presence of the perforated page is a clear indicator that hidden-message communication is occurring, and it is caught if either party is searched
It cannot hide any message
It requires the same book for sender and receiver
questions.e: The template cipher is both difficult to execute and easy to detect: the presence of the perforated page is a clear indicator that hidden-message communication is occurring, so it fails if either party is physically searched.

questions.q: What is the primary purpose of a hash function in information security?
o: To encrypt a message so only the recipient can read it
To confirm the identity of a specific message and confirm that its content has not been changed
To compress a file to save space
To distribute keys between parties
questions.e: Hash functions are mathematical algorithms used to confirm the identity of a specific message and to confirm that the content has not been changed.

questions.q: A hash algorithm converts a variable-length message into what, and what is that value also called?
o: A variable-length ciphertext; a signature
A single fixed-length value; a message digest (a fingerprint of the message)
A public/private key pair; a certificate
A shifted alphabet; a cipher
questions.e: A hash algorithm creates a hash value, also known as a message digest, by converting variable-length messages into a single fixed-length value — a fingerprint of the author's message.

questions.q: Why are hash functions described as 'one-way' operations?
o: Because they can only encrypt, never decrypt
Because the same message always yields the same hash, but the hash value cannot be used to determine the contents of the message
Because they require a public and a private key
Because they change every time they run
questions.e: Hash functions are one-way operations: the same message always provides the same hash value, but the hash value itself cannot be used to determine the contents of the message.

questions.q: What is a message authentication code (MAC) in the context of hashing?
o: A random salt added to a password
A key-dependent, one-way hash function that allows only specific recipients (symmetric key holders) to access the message digest
A public-key certificate
The physical address of a network card
questions.e: A MAC is a key-dependent, one-way hash function that allows only specific recipients (symmetric key holders) to access the message digest; hashing itself does not require keys, but a MAC can be attached.

questions.q: How are hash functions used in password verification systems?
o: They store the plaintext password for comparison
The hash (message digest) of the original password is stored; at login the system hashes the input and compares it to the stored value
They encrypt the password with the user's public key
They transmit the password over the network in clear text
questions.e: Because hash functions are one-way, password systems store the hash of the originally issued password; when the user logs on, the system hashes the input password and compares it against the stored value to confirm identity.

questions.q: The Secure Hash Standard (SHS) is issued by NIST. According to FIPS 180-4, how large a message digest does SHA-1 produce?
o: 128-bit
160-bit
256-bit
512-bit
questions.e: FIPS 180-4 specifies SHA-1 (Secure Hash Algorithm 1), which produces a 160-bit message digest that can be used as input to a digital signature algorithm.

questions.q: SHA-1 is based on principles modeled after MD4, which is part of a family of hash algorithms created by whom?
o: Whitfield Diffie
Ronald Rivest
Tony Hoare
Joe Jarzombek
questions.e: SHA-1 is based on principles modeled after MD4, which is part of the MDx family of hash algorithms created by Ronald Rivest.

questions.q: In a hash algorithm, the number of bits used is a measurement of the algorithm's strength against what kind of attack?
o: Brute-force key attacks
Collision attacks
Denial-of-service attacks
Social engineering attacks
questions.e: The number of bits used in the hash algorithm is a measurement of the algorithm's strength against collision attacks; SHA-256, SHA-384, and SHA-512 were proposed as stronger standards.

questions.q: What is rainbow cracking, and what does it use?
o: A brute-force attack that tries every password from scratch
A time-memory trade-off attack that uses a rainbow table — a database of precomputed hashes — to look up a hashed password and read out its text version with no brute force required
A social-engineering attack via e-mail
A denial-of-service flood
questions.e: Rainbow cracking uses a rainbow table — a database of precomputed hashes from sequentially calculated passwords — so the cracker simply looks up the hashed password and reads the text version, requiring no brute force. It is properly classified as a time-memory trade-off attack.

questions.q: What is password hash salting?
o: Repeatedly hashing a password thousands of times
The process of providing a random piece of data to the hashing function when the hash is first calculated
Increasing the key length from 128 to 256 bits
Storing passwords in plaintext
questions.e: Salting is the process of providing a random piece of data to the hashing function when the hash is first calculated; it defends against rainbow-table attacks because precomputed tables no longer match the salted hashes.

questions.q: What is the difference between key stretching and key strengthening?
o: Key stretching lengthens the key; key strengthening repeats the hash

Key stretching transforms a weak key into a stronger one via a computationally intensive process (e.g. iterative hashing, PBKDF2, bcrypt, Argon2); key strengthening improves the inherent strength of a key itself, often by increasing its length or entropy
They are identical
Key stretching uses public keys; key strengthening uses private keys
questions.e: Key stretching transforms a weak key into a stronger one by applying a computationally intensive process (iterative hashing, PBKDF2, bcrypt, Argon2); key strengthening improves the inherent strength of a key itself, for example by increasing its length (128 to 256 bits) or using high-entropy sources.

questions.q: Which algorithms are named examples of key-stretching functions that take a password and generate a derived key using salting and multiple iterations?
o: AES, DES, and 3DES
PBKDF2, bcrypt, and Argon2
RSA, ECC, and Diffie-Hellman
SHA-1, MD4, and MD5
questions.e: PBKDF2, bcrypt, and Argon2 are key-stretching algorithms that take a password and generate a derived key using techniques like salting and multiple iterations to increase the cost of cracking.

questions.q: The two broad categories of cryptographic algorithms are distinguished by what?
o: The length of their output
The types of keys they use for encryption and decryption operations
The speed at which they run
Whether they are patented
questions.e: Cryptographic algorithms fall into two broad categories — symmetric and asymmetric — distinguished by the types of keys they use for encryption and decryption operations.

questions.q: What defines symmetric encryption?
o: It uses two different but related keys
It requires the same secret key to both encipher and decipher the message (also called private-key encryption)
It uses no keys at all
It uses a public key to encrypt and a private key to decrypt
questions.e: Symmetric encryption requires the same secret key to both encipher and decipher the message; it is also called private-key encryption and uses fast mathematical operations.

questions.q: Which of the following are popular symmetric encryption standards?
o: RSA, ECC, and Diffie-Hellman
DES, Triple DES (3DES), and AES
SHA-1, SHA-256, and MD4
TLS, SSH, and IPsec
questions.e: Popular symmetric encryption methods include the Data Encryption Standard (DES), Triple DES (3DES), and the Advanced Encryption Standard (AES).

questions.q: On what date was AES approved by the U.S. Secretary of Commerce as the official federal governmental standard?
o: January 1, 2000
September 11, 2001
April 8, 2014
questions.e: AES was approved by the Secretary of Commerce as the official federal governmental standard on May 26, 2002, following a selection process involving the U.S. government, private industry, and academia.

questions.q: In asymmetric encryption, if key A is used to encrypt a message, which key can decrypt it?
o: Key A
Only key B
Any key
No key can decrypt it
questions.e: Asymmetric encryption uses two different but related keys: if key A is used to encrypt the message, only key B can decrypt it, and if key B encrypts, only key A can decrypt.

questions.q: What is the more common name for asymmetric encryption, and why?
o: Private-key encryption, because both keys are secret
Public-key encryption, because one key is kept private (secret) while the other is a public key stored where anyone can use it
Hybrid encryption, because it mixes two ciphers
Symmetric encryption, because the keys are equal
questions.e: Asymmetric encryption is more commonly called public-key encryption: one key is a private key kept secret by the owner, and the other is a public key stored in a public location where anyone can use it.

questions.q: One of the most popular public-key cryptosystems is RSA. From what is its name derived?
o: The three keys it uses
Rivest-Shamir-Adleman, the algorithm's developers
Really Secure Algorithm
The RSA Corporation's founding date
questions.e: RSA is named after Rivest-Shamir-Adleman, the algorithm's developers; it is embedded in essentially all widely available Web browsers and is the de facto standard for public-use encryption.

questions.q: Why is a single conversation between two parties using pure asymmetric encryption considered inefficient?
o: Because it uses the same key for both parties
Because holding one conversation between two parties requires four keys, and the number of keys grows confusingly as more parties join; it is also less CPU-efficient than symmetric encryption
Because asymmetric encryption cannot provide confidentiality
Because it requires a book as the key
questions.e: A single conversation between two parties requires four keys, and managing which public key encrypts which message becomes confusing as more organizations join; asymmetric encryption is also less CPU-efficient than symmetric encryption, so hybrid systems like PKI are more commonly used.

questions.q: To crack an encryption key of k bits using a brute-force attack, a computer must perform a maximum of how many operations?
o: k operations
2k operations
2^k operations
k^2 operations
questions.e: To crack a k-bit encryption key by brute force, a computer needs to perform a maximum of 2^k operations (2^k guesses), where k is the number of bits in the key.

questions.q: Because pure asymmetric systems are inefficient, which type of system is more commonly used in practice?
o: Caesar ciphers
Hybrid systems such as public key infrastructure (PKI)
Book ciphers
Template ciphers
questions.e: Because pure asymmetric encryption is inefficient in key management and CPU computation, hybrid systems such as public key infrastructure (PKI) are more commonly used than pure asymmetric systems.

questions.q: Secure communication protocols are said to ensure which four properties?
o: Speed, cost, usability, and scalability
Confidentiality, Integrity, Authenticity, and Non-Repudiation
Encryption, hashing, signing, and compression
Availability, reliability, portability, and maintainability
questions.e: Protocols for secure communication ensure Confidentiality, Integrity, Authenticity, and Non-Repudiation, protecting data in transit across untrusted networks.

questions.q: Which cryptographic primitive provides fast encryption of bulk data using a shared secret key, and provides Confidentiality?
o: Asymmetric encryption (RSA)
Symmetric encryption (AES)
Cryptographic hash functions (SHA-256)
Message Authentication Code (HMAC)
questions.e: Symmetric encryption (e.g. AES) provides fast encryption for bulk data using a shared secret key and provides Confidentiality; asymmetric encryption solves key distribution, hashes provide integrity, and HMAC provides integrity plus authentication.

questions.q: What does an HMAC (a hash combined with a secret key) provide?
o: Only confidentiality
Both Integrity and Authentication (proving data is unchanged and came from someone with the key)
Only key exchange
Only non-repudiation
questions.e: An HMAC (Message Authentication Code) is a hash combined with a secret key; it proves both that the data is unchanged (integrity) and that it came from someone who holds the key (authentication).

questions.q: TLS (Transport Layer Security) secures HTTP traffic by turning it into what?
o: FTP
HTTPS
SMTP
SSH
questions.e: TLS is the most important protocol on the internet; it secures HTTP traffic, turning it into HTTPS, and is what places the lock icon in the browser.

questions.q: During the TLS handshake, what does the server present to prove its identity, and who issues it?
o: A password, issued by the browser
A digital certificate containing the server's public key, issued by a trusted Certificate Authority (CA)
A rainbow table, issued by NIST
A private key, issued by the client
questions.e: In the TLS handshake the server sends a digital certificate, issued by a trusted Certificate Authority (CA) such as DigiCert, which contains the server's public key and proves the server's identity.

questions.q: During the TLS handshake, how is the pre-master secret protected when the browser sends it to the server?
o: It is sent in plain text
It is encrypted with the server's public key so that only the server, with its private key, can decrypt it
It is hashed with SHA-256
It is signed with the browser's private key
questions.e: The browser generates a pre-master secret, encrypts it with the server's public key from the certificate, and sends it back; only the server with its matching private key can decrypt it. Both sides then derive the same symmetric session keys.

questions.q: After the TLS handshake establishes session keys, how is subsequent data protected?
o: With slow asymmetric (public-key) encryption
At high speed with symmetric session keys (e.g. using AES)
With a book cipher
It is sent unencrypted
questions.e: After the handshake, all subsequent data for the session is encrypted at high speed using the symmetric session keys (e.g. AES); asymmetric encryption is used only to exchange the secret securely.

questions.q: What is SSH (Secure Shell) used for, and what stronger authentication does it offer besides passwords?
o: Securing web browsing; certificate authentication
Secure remote login and command execution on a server; public-key cryptography (essentially password-less login)
Encrypting entire networks; AH and ESP
Real-time media; DTLS
questions.e: SSH is a protocol for secure remote login and command execution on a server, the standard way admins manage servers. Besides password authentication, it supports more secure public-key cryptography, where the client proves it holds the private key matching a public key on the server (password-less login).

questions.q: How does IPsec differ from TLS and SSH in what it secures?
o: IPsec secures a single browser session
IPsec secures all network traffic at the IP layer by encrypting and authenticating each IP packet, commonly used in VPNs to create secure tunnels
IPsec secures only e-mail
IPsec secures only real-time media
questions.e: While TLS secures a single application and SSH secures a single login session, IPsec secures all network traffic at the IP layer by encrypting and authenticating each IP packet, commonly used in Virtual Private Networks (VPNs) to create secure tunnels over public networks.

questions.q: What is the difference between the two main IPsec protocols, AH and ESP?
o: AH encrypts the payload; ESP only authenticates

Authentication Header (AH) provides integrity and authentication for the entire IP packet; Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP) provides confidentiality, integrity, and authentication for the payload (it encrypts the data)
AH is for VPNs; ESP is for e-mail
They are identical
questions.e: Authentication Header (AH) provides integrity and authentication for the entire IP packet (header + data) but does not encrypt; Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP) provides confidentiality, integrity, and authentication for the payload by encrypting the data.

questions.q: What does the Diffie-Hellman key exchange achieve, and on what hard mathematical problem does its security rely?
o: It signs messages; the factoring problem

It lets two parties securely agree on a shared secret key over a public channel; its security relies on modular exponentiation being easy to compute but hard to reverse (the discrete logarithm problem)
It hashes passwords; the collision problem
It compresses data; the halting problem
questions.e: Diffie-Hellman is a method for two parties to securely agree on a shared secret key over a public channel; it relies on modular exponentiation, which is easy to compute but extremely difficult to reverse (the discrete logarithm problem), so an eavesdropper cannot determine the private numbers.

questions.q: What is Perfect Forward Secrecy (PFS)?
o: A property where the same key is reused for every session
A property where the compromise of long-term private keys does not let an attacker decrypt past recorded sessions
A property that makes certificates never expire
A property of symmetric encryption only
questions.e: Perfect Forward Secrecy (PFS) is a property where the compromise of long-term private keys (such as a server key) does not let an attacker decrypt previously recorded sessions; enabling (EC)DHE/ECDHE key exchange in TLS provides PFS.

questions.q: What is Public Key Infrastructure (PKI)?
o: A single encryption algorithm
The people, processes, and software that create, issue, validate, and revoke digital certificates so identities can be trusted on the internet
A type of symmetric cipher
A denial-of-service defense
questions.e: PKI is the whole system of people, processes, and software that create, issue, validate, and revoke digital certificates, so identities can be trusted; it involves certificates, Certificate Authorities (CAs), revocation, and policies.

questions.q: What is the difference between OCSP and a CRL for checking certificate revocation?
o: OCSP is an older downloaded list; CRL is a live query

OCSP (Online Certificate Status Protocol) is a live check asking a responder whether a certificate is revoked; a CRL (Certificate Revocation List) is a published list of revoked certificates that clients download and check
They are identical
OCSP checks passwords; CRL checks certificates
questions.e: OCSP (Online Certificate Status Protocol) is a live query to a responder about whether a certificate is revoked; a CRL (Certificate Revocation List) is a published list of revoked certificates that clients download. CRLs are older; OCSP or OCSP stapling is preferred.

questions.q: What does OCSP stapling do?
o: It downloads the entire CRL to the client
The server attaches a recent OCSP response (signed by the CA) to the TLS handshake so the client doesn't have to query the CA itself
It disables revocation checking
It encrypts the certificate
questions.e: With OCSP stapling, the server attaches a recent, CA-signed OCSP response to the TLS handshake, so the client can confirm the certificate is not revoked without extra round-trips to the CA.

questions.q: What does HSTS (HTTP Strict Transport Security) do?
o: It encrypts the payload of IP packets
It is a browser policy (sent via a header) that tells browsers to only ever use HTTPS to access a site for a specified time
It issues digital certificates
It derives session keys
questions.e: HSTS is a browser policy, sent via a header, that tells browsers to only ever use HTTPS to access a site for a specified number of seconds, so they never fall back to insecure HTTP.

questions.q: What is an AEAD cipher (e.g. AES-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305)?
o: A cipher that only hashes data
A cipher that encrypts data and also guarantees integrity/authenticity in one operation
A cipher that only exchanges keys
A cipher that requires no key
questions.e: An AEAD (Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data) cipher, such as AES-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305, encrypts data and also guarantees its integrity and authenticity in a single operation, like a locked box with a tamper-evident seal.

questions.q: What is a JWT (JSON Web Token), and what precaution is stressed for it?
o: A symmetric key; it must be reused
A compact, signed token representing claims about a user, used for stateless authentication; it must always travel over HTTPS/TLS
A certificate revocation list; it must be downloaded
A type of firewall; it must be air-gapped
questions.e: A JWT is a compact, signed (and optionally encrypted) token representing claims about a user, commonly used for stateless authentication; it must always be sent over HTTPS/TLS, and sensitive secrets should not be stored in its payload.

questions.q: What does OAuth2 provide?
o: Encryption of IP packets
An authorization framework for delegated access, letting third parties get limited access to resources without sharing passwords (often via tokens)
A hashing algorithm for passwords
A physical security control
questions.e: OAuth2 is an authorization framework for delegated access: third parties can be granted limited access to resources without the user sharing their password, typically by issuing tokens (analogy: a valet key).

questions.q: What is PCI-DSS?
o: A wireless encryption standard
The Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard — rules companies must follow when handling cardholder data to reduce fraud risk
A key derivation function
A certificate authority
questions.e: PCI-DSS (Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard) is a set of rules companies must follow when handling cardholder data (cards, payment processing) to reduce fraud risk; using a third-party gateway or tokenization keeps PCI scope small.

questions.q: What is the difference between WPA2 and WPA3 for Wi-Fi security?
o: WPA2 is newer and stronger than WPA3
WPA3 is the newer, stronger standard with better protections (such as SAE and an improved handshake); WPA2 is the older standard
They are identical
WPA2 is for wired networks; WPA3 is for wireless
questions.e: WPA2 and WPA3 are Wi-Fi Protected Access standards; WPA3 is the newer, stronger standard with better protections (SAE, improved handshake and guest handling), so it is recommended for new deployments.

questions.q: What is the primary mission of an information security program?
o: To maximise the speed of the organization's systems
To ensure that information assets — information and the systems that house them — remain safe and useful
To eliminate the need for employees
To generate profit for the organization
questions.e: The primary mission of an information security program is to ensure that information assets — information and the systems that house them — remain safe and useful.

questions.q: Information security performs four important functions for an organization. Which set lists them?
o: Encrypting, hashing, signing, and auditing

Protecting the organization's ability to function; protecting the data and information it collects and uses; enabling the safe operation of applications; and safeguarding the organization's technology assets
Investigation, analysis, design, and implementation
Confidentiality, integrity, availability, and non-repudiation
questions.e: The four functions are: protecting the organization's ability to function; protecting the data and information the organization collects and uses (physical or electronic); enabling the safe operation of applications running on its IT systems; and safeguarding the organization's technology assets.

questions.q: What is the distinction between a threat and an attack?
o: A threat is an ongoing act; an attack is a potential risk
A threat is a potential risk to an information asset (always present); an attack is an ongoing act against the asset that could result in a loss (exists only during the act)
They are the same thing
A threat only applies to hardware; an attack only to software
questions.e: A threat represents a potential risk to an information asset and is always present; an attack represents an ongoing act against the asset that could result in a loss and exists only when a specific act may cause a loss (like a thunderstorm threat present all summer vs. an attack only during an actual storm).

questions.q: How many general categories of threats to information assets are described in the standard scheme?
questions.e: The standard scheme consists of 12 general categories of threats representing a clear and present danger to an organization's people, information, and systems.

questions.q: Which category of threat has 'espionage or trespass' as its type, with the example 'unauthorized access and/or data collection'?
o: Forces of nature
Espionage or trespass
Human error or failure
Theft
questions.e: 'Espionage or trespass' is one of the 12 categories, with the attack example 'unauthorized access and/or data collection'.

questions.q: What is intellectual property (IP)?
o: Any physical property owned by an organization
The creation, ownership, and control of original ideas as well as the representation of those ideas
The set of an organization's employees
A category of network hardware
questions.e: Intellectual property (IP) is the creation, ownership, and control of original ideas as well as the representation of those ideas; IP includes trade secrets, copyrights, trademarks, and patents.

questions.q: What is the most common breach of intellectual property?
o: Physical theft of hardware
Software piracy — the unlawful use or duplication of software-based intellectual property
Denial-of-service attacks
Social engineering
questions.e: The most common IP breach is the unlawful use or duplication of software-based intellectual property, commonly known as software piracy; because most software is licensed to a particular purchaser, copying it without a license violates the copyright.

questions.q: Which two watchdog organizations investigate allegations of software abuse?
o: NIST and ISO
The Software & Information Industry Association (SIIA) and the Business Software Alliance (BSA)
OWASP and SANS
The FBI and DHS
questions.e: Two watchdog organizations investigate software abuse: the Software & Information Industry Association (SIIA) and the Business Software Alliance (BSA).

questions.q: What is social engineering?
o: Using engineering tools to build secure software
The process of using social skills to convince people to reveal access credentials or other valuable information to an attacker
A method of encrypting social media data
The design of social networks
questions.e: Social engineering is the process of using social skills to convince people to reveal access credentials or other valuable information to an attacker.

questions.q: What is phishing?
o: A denial-of-service attack that floods a server

A form of social engineering in which the attacker sends an apparently legitimate communication (usually e-mail) containing hidden code that redirects the reply to a third-party site to extract personal or confidential information
A technique for cracking hashed passwords
The physical theft of equipment
questions.e: Phishing is a form of social engineering in which the attacker provides what appears to be a legitimate communication (usually e-mail) but which contains hidden or embedded code that redirects the reply to a third-party site to extract personal or confidential information.

questions.q: What is the difference between a virus and a worm?
o: A virus replicates without attaching to a program; a worm attaches to programs
A virus is attached to other executable programs and replicates when activated; a worm is capable of activation and replication without being attached to an existing program
They are identical
A virus only affects hardware; a worm only affects software
questions.e: A virus is a type of malware attached to other executable programs that replicates and propagates when activated; a worm is capable of activation and replication without being attached to an existing program.

questions.q: What is a Trojan horse?
o: Malware that changes its appearance over time to avoid signature detection
A malware program that hides its true nature and reveals its designed behavior only when activated
A back door left by a system designer
A flood of connection requests
questions.e: A Trojan horse is a malware program that hides its true nature and reveals its designed (malicious) behavior only when activated. (Malware that changes its appearance to evade signatures is a polymorphic threat.)

questions.q: What distinguishes a distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attack from an ordinary DoS attack?
o: A DDoS uses encryption; a DoS does not
In a DoS the attacker sends many requests from one source, while a DDoS launches a coordinated stream of requests against a target from many locations at the same time
A DDoS targets hardware; a DoS targets software
They are the same
questions.e: In a denial-of-service (DoS) attack, a single attacker overwhelms a target with connection or information requests; in a distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attack, a coordinated stream of requests is launched against a target from many locations simultaneously (using compromised machines called bots or zombies).

questions.q: What is the difference between phishing and pharming?
o: Phishing redirects traffic silently; pharming requires a click

Phishing requires the user to actively click a link, whereas pharming redirects legitimate user Web traffic to illegitimate Web sites (e.g. via DNS cache poisoning) without the user's active participation
They are identical
Phishing targets networks; pharming targets e-mail
questions.e: Phishing requires the user to actively click a link or button, while pharming is the redirection of legitimate user Web traffic to illegitimate Web sites (for example via DNS cache poisoning) to collect personal information, without the user's active participation.

questions.q: What is ransomware?
o: Software that secretly gathers user information
Computer software specifically designed to identify and encrypt valuable information in a victim's system in order to extort payment for the key needed to unlock the encryption
Unsolicited commercial e-mail
A forged source IP address
questions.e: Ransomware is computer software designed to identify and encrypt valuable information in a victim's system in order to extort payment for the key needed to unlock the encryption; it is a form of information extortion.

questions.q: What is a man-in-the-middle attack?
o: An attack that floods a server with requests
An attack in which the attacker monitors (sniffs) packets from the network, modifies them, and inserts them back into the network
The physical theft of a server
A social-engineering phone call
questions.e: In a man-in-the-middle attack, an attacker monitors (or sniffs) packets from the network, modifies them, and inserts them back into the network, intercepting communications between two parties.

questions.q: The OWASP 'Top 10' for 2021 lists which risk as number one?
o: Injection
Broken Access Control
Cross-Site Scripting
Security Misconfiguration
questions.e: In the OWASP (Open Web Application Security Project) Top 10 for 2021 — the ten most critical web application security risks — Broken Access Control is ranked number one.

questions.q: What is spoofing?
o: Encrypting a message with the wrong key
A technique for gaining unauthorized access to computers using a forged or modified source IP address to make messages appear to come from a trusted host
A method of hashing passwords
A denial-of-service flood
questions.e: Spoofing is a technique for gaining unauthorized access to computers using a forged or modified source IP address to give the perception that messages are coming from a trusted host.

questions.q: How are laws defined in the context of information security?
o: The fixed moral attitudes of a particular group
Rules that mandate or prohibit certain behavior and are enforced by the state
Voluntary guidelines with no penalties
The branch of philosophy studying moral judgment
questions.e: Laws are rules that mandate or prohibit certain behavior and are enforced by the state. Ethics, by contrast, is the branch of philosophy that considers the nature, criteria, sources, logic, and validity of moral judgment.

questions.q: What is the key difference in the basis of authority between law and ethics?
o: Laws are based on cultural morals; ethics carry the authority of a governing body
Laws carry the authority of a governing body; ethics are based on cultural mores (moral attitudes)
Both are enforced identically by the state
Neither has any basis of authority
questions.e: Laws carry the authority of a governing body, whereas ethics are based on cultural mores — the fixed moral attitudes or customs of a particular group.

questions.q: What is the difference between due care and due diligence?
o: Due care is a legal penalty; due diligence is a reward

Due care refers to the measures an organization takes to ensure every employee knows what is acceptable; due diligence refers to the reasonable steps taken to meet the obligations imposed by laws or regulations
They are identical
Due care applies to hardware; due diligence to software
questions.e: Due care refers to the measures an organization takes to ensure every employee knows what is acceptable and what is not; due diligence refers to the reasonable steps taken by people or organizations to meet the obligations imposed by laws or regulations.

questions.q: What is 'long-arm jurisdiction'?
o: The power to make legal decisions within a fixed area only
The ability of a legal entity to exercise its influence beyond its normal boundaries by asserting a connection between an out-of-jurisdiction entity and a local legal case
A legal requirement to make compensation for a loss
An entity's legal obligation or responsibility
questions.e: Long-arm jurisdiction is the ability of a legal entity to exercise its influence beyond its normal boundaries by asserting a connection between an out-of-jurisdiction entity and a local legal case. (Liability is the legal obligation; restitution is the requirement to make compensation.)

questions.q: What is liability in the legal sense, and can an employer be held liable for an employee's acts?
o: Liability is a reward; employers are never liable
Liability is an entity's legal obligation or responsibility, and an employer can be held financially liable for an employee's acts regardless of whether it authorized them
Liability is a moral custom with no legal force
Liability applies only to individuals, never organizations
questions.e: Liability is an entity's legal obligation or responsibility; it includes the obligation to make restitution for wrongs committed, and an employer can be held financially liable regardless of whether it authorized the act.

questions.q: What is a key distinction between organizational policies and laws?
o: Ignorance of a policy is never an acceptable defense, like ignorance of law
Laws are legally binding and enforceable in court, whereas policies are guidelines that are not legally enforceable and for which ignorance can be an acceptable defense
Policies are enforced by the state; laws by the organization
There is no difference
questions.e: Laws are legally binding and enforceable in court; policies are organizational guidelines that are not legally enforceable. A notable contrast: ignorance of the law is no excuse, but ignorance of a policy IS an acceptable defense.

questions.q: For a policy to be enforceable, five conditions must be met. Which set correctly lists them?
o: Encryption, hashing, signing, auditing, and logging
Dissemination, Review, Comprehension, Compliance, and Uniform enforcement
Investigation, analysis, design, implementation, and maintenance
Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, and Recover
questions.e: The five policy-enforcement criteria are Dissemination (distribution), Review (reading), Comprehension (understanding), Compliance (agreement), and Uniform enforcement. Only when all five are met can an organization penalize violators without fear of legal retribution.

questions.q: In the policy-enforcement criteria, the 'Comprehension' requirement is typically demonstrated using what technique?
o: Logon banners
Quizzes and other assessments
Hard-copy distribution
Recordings in alternate languages
questions.e: Comprehension (understanding) requires that the employee understands the policy's requirements, which is typically demonstrated using quizzes and other assessments. Compliance (agreement) is often shown via logon banners or a signed document.

questions.q: Which of the following is a subtype of public law?
o: Contract law
Constitutional law
Tort law
Property law
questions.e: Public law governs the relationship between individuals and government; its subtypes include constitutional law, administrative law, and criminal law. Contract, tort, property, and family law are subtypes of private (civil) law.

questions.q: What distinguishes criminal law from civil (private) law?
o: Criminal law resolves disputes between private individuals
Criminal law defines offenses against society and their punishments, with the government initiating prosecution; civil law addresses disputes between individuals or private organizations
They are the same
Civil law only applies to corporations
questions.e: Criminal law defines offenses and their punishments to maintain public order — crimes are treated as acts against society and the government initiates prosecution; civil (private) law addresses disputes between individuals or private organizations, such as contract and tort law.

questions.q: In a common-law legal system, how is law primarily shaped?
o: Entirely by written codes enacted by a legislature
By courts through judicial decisions, creating legally binding precedents
By religious texts and principles
By long-standing oral customs only
questions.e: In common law, courts actively shape the law through judicial decisions, creating legally binding precedents. Statutory law is formally written and enacted by a legislative body, while a civil-law system relies on comprehensive codes rather than judicial precedent.

questions.q: In the Pegasus spyware case study, what is the NSO Group, and what action did the U.S. take in 2021?
o: A U.S. antivirus firm that was awarded a contract
An Israeli cyber-arms firm that developed the Pegasus spyware; in 2021 the U.S. government blacklisted NSO Group, citing 'transnational repression'
A European certificate authority that was certified
A watchdog organization that investigates piracy
questions.e: The NSO Group is an Israeli cyber-arms firm that developed Pegasus spyware, which covertly infects mobile phones and collects personal data; in 2021 the U.S. government blacklisted NSO Group, citing 'transnational repression'.

questions.q: What is punitive damages, as awarded in civil courts?
o: Compensation exactly equal to the loss suffered
A punishment assessed as a deterrent to future transgressions
A refund of legal fees
A moral custom with no monetary value
questions.e: Punitive damages are a punishment assessed as a deterrent to future transgressions; laws are sometimes enforced in civil courts, where large damages can be awarded to plaintiffs.

questions.q: What is cyber crime?
o: Only the physical theft of computers
Activity in which computers or networks are a tool, a target, or a place of criminal activity
The legal use of computers for business
A type of encryption algorithm
questions.e: Cyber crime is activity in which computers or networks are a tool, a target, or a place of criminal activity — any use of a computer as an instrument to further illegal ends such as fraud, identity theft, or violating privacy.

questions.q: What is Pakistan's primary comprehensive law for electronic crimes?
o: The Electronic Transaction Ordinance 2002
The Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act (PECA), 2016
The Pakistan Electronic Crime Ordinance 2007
The Citizens Protection (Against Online Harm) Rules, 2020
questions.e: The Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act (PECA), 2016 is Pakistan's comprehensive legal framework for the investigation, prosecution, and adjudication of electronic crimes, defining offences such as unauthorized access, cyber terrorism, electronic fraud, and hate speech.

questions.q: What was the Electronic Transaction Ordinance (ETO) 2002 in Pakistan?
o: The law that created the FIA
The first IT-relevant legislation created by national lawmakers, providing the foundation for legal recognition of Pakistani e-commerce
A law regulating social media companies
The successor to PECA 2016
questions.e: The Electronic Transaction Ordinance (ETO) 2002 was the first IT-relevant legislation created by Pakistani national lawmakers; it was the first step providing legal sanctity and protection for Pakistani e-commerce, giving recognition to electronic documents, records, and signatures.

questions.q: Under PECA 2016, cyber terrorism (Section 10) carries which maximum punishment?
o: Three months imprisonment or a fifty-thousand-rupee fine
Fourteen years imprisonment or a fine up to fifty million rupees, or both
One year imprisonment or a one-million-rupee fine
A fine only, with no imprisonment
questions.e: Under PECA 2016 Section 10, cyber terrorism carries imprisonment up to fourteen years or a fine up to fifty million rupees, or both — the highest penalties in the Act.

questions.q: Under PECA 2016, unauthorized access to an information system or data (Section 3) carries which maximum penalty?
o: Imprisonment up to three months or a fine up to fifty thousand rupees, or both
Imprisonment up to fourteen years
Imprisonment up to seven years or a fine up to five million rupees
The death penalty
questions.e: Under PECA 2016 Section 3, unauthorized access to an information system or data carries imprisonment up to three months, or a fine up to fifty thousand rupees, or both.

questions.q: What happened to the Pakistan Electronic Crime Ordinance (PECO) 2007?
o: It was upgraded into PECA 2016 unchanged
As an ordinance promulgated in 2007, it lapsed (expired) in 2009; it was criticised for giving excessive powers to the FIA
It is still Pakistan's primary cyber law
It was never enacted
questions.e: The Pakistan Electronic Crime Ordinance (PECO) 2007, promulgated as an ordinance, lapsed in 2009; it drew criticism because innocent people could be framed and it gave excessive powers to the Federal Investigation Agency (FIA), covering 17 types of cyber crimes with penalties from six months' imprisonment to capital punishment.

questions.q: The Council of Europe Convention on Cybercrime (Budapest Convention) is best described as what?
o: A purely American law
The first and most comprehensive international treaty on cybercrime, adopted in 2001, aiming to standardize cybercrime laws across nations
A wireless encryption standard
Pakistan's primary cyber law
questions.e: The Council of Europe Convention on Cybercrime (Budapest Convention), adopted in 2001, is the first and most comprehensive international treaty on cybercrime; it harmonizes national laws, improves investigative techniques, and increases international cooperation.

questions.q: The Agreement on Trade-Related Aspects of Intellectual Property Rights (TRIPS) was created by which body, and what was its significance?
o: NIST; the first hashing standard
The World Trade Organization (WTO); the first significant international effort to protect intellectual property rights
The Council of Europe; a wireless standard
The FIA; Pakistan's e-commerce law
questions.e: TRIPS, created by the World Trade Organization (WTO) and negotiated from 1986 to 1994, was the first significant international effort to protect intellectual property rights.

questions.q: What is the U.S. Digital Millennium Copyright Act (DMCA) primarily concerned with?
o: Regulating Wi-Fi encryption
Copyright infringement in the digital realm, including prohibiting the circumvention of technological protections controlling access to copyrighted content
Defining the phases of the SDLC
Protecting cardholder data
questions.e: The DMCA is the American contribution to an international WIPO effort; it addresses digital copyright, prohibiting circumvention of protections that control access to protected content, banning devices used to circumvent them, and prohibiting alteration of copyright information.

questions.q: Under the EU's General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), what is the maximum fine?
o: €1 million or 1% of turnover
Up to €20 million or 4% of global annual turnover, whichever is higher
$52.2 billion
Fifty million rupees
questions.e: GDPR (the EU's data protection and privacy regulation) provides for fines up to €20 million or 4% of global annual turnover, whichever is higher, and has extraterritorial reach.

questions.q: The U.K. Computer Misuse Act 1990 defined how many computer misuse offenses?
o: One
Two
Three
Ten
questions.e: The U.K. Computer Misuse Act 1990 defined three computer misuse offenses: unauthorized access to computer material; unauthorized access with intent to commit or facilitate further offenses; and unauthorized acts with intent to impair (or recklessness as to impairing) the operation of a computer.

questions.q: The (ISC)2 Code of Ethics contains four mandatory canons. Which is one of them?
o: Maximise shareholder profit
Protect society, the commonwealth, and the infrastructure
Report all colleagues to authorities
Never use encryption
questions.e: The (ISC)2 Code of Ethics has four mandatory canons: protect society, the commonwealth, and the infrastructure; act honorably, honestly, justly, responsibly, and legally; provide diligent and competent service to principals; and advance and protect the profession.

questions.q: The ACM (Association for Computing Machinery) was established in which year, and how is it described?
o: 1990; a payment card standards body
1947; the world's first educational and scientific computing society
2001; an international cybercrime task force
2016; Pakistan's cyber authority
questions.e: The ACM was established in 1947 as the world's first educational and scientific computing society; its code requires its members to act ethically, addressing confidentiality, causing no harm (specifically viruses), privacy, and intellectual property.

questions.q: Do the IT and information security fields have binding codes of ethics comparable to medicine and law?
o: Yes, enforced by the state like medicine and law
No; unlike medicine and law, they do not have binding codes of ethics — professional associations and certification agencies maintain codes but cannot banish violators from practicing
Yes, enforced by NIST
No codes of ethics exist at all
questions.e: Unlike medicine and law, the IT and information security fields do not have binding codes of ethics; professional associations (ACM, ISSA) and certification agencies ((ISC)2, ISACA) maintain ethical codes but cannot banish violators from practicing.

questions.q: Deterrence of illegal or unethical behavior works best only when three conditions are present. Which set lists them?
o: Encryption, hashing, and signing
Fear of penalty; probability of being apprehended; and probability of the penalty being applied
Dissemination, review, and comprehension
Confidentiality, integrity, and availability
questions.e: Laws, policies, and penalties deter behavior only if three conditions are present: fear of the penalty, the probability of being apprehended, and the probability of the penalty being applied.

questions.q: The three general causes of unethical and illegal behavior are which of the following?
o: Malware, phishing, and spoofing
Ignorance, accident, and intent
Bottom-up, top-down, and grassroots
Confidentiality, integrity, and availability
questions.e: The three general causes of unethical and illegal behavior are ignorance, accident, and intent; the first deterrence method against ignorance is education.

questions.q: What is the difference between strategic, tactical, and operational plans?
o: They are three names for the same plan
Strategic plans set long-term direction; tactical plans are short-term undertakings completed within one or two years; operational plans organize ongoing day-to-day tasks
Strategic plans are daily; operational plans are long-term
They differ only in who signs them
questions.e: A strategic plan is the long-term direction of the organization; a tactical plan is a short-term undertaking completed within one or two years; and an operational plan is derived from tactical planning to organize the ongoing, day-to-day performance of tasks. Strategic plans create tactical plans, which create operational plans.

questions.q: What is information security governance?
o: The technical configuration of firewalls
The strategic controlling function of an organization's senior management — controlling or governing the processes used to accomplish objectives
The daily work of systems administrators
A hashing standard
questions.e: Governance describes the entire function of controlling, or governing, the processes used by a group to accomplish some objective; information security governance represents the strategic controlling function of an organization's senior management.

questions.q: Security policy is described as which kind of control?
o: The most expensive control that is easy to implement
The least expensive control to execute, but the most difficult to implement properly
A purely technical control requiring no management effort
An optional control with no legal standing
questions.e: Security policies are the least expensive control to execute (creation and dissemination require only management time and effort), but the most difficult to implement properly.

questions.q: According to NIST SP 800-14, management must define which three types of security policy?
o: Managerial, operational, and technical policies
Enterprise information security policy (EISP), issue-specific security policy (ISSP), and systems-specific security policy (SysSP)
Strategic, tactical, and operational policies
Public, private, and hybrid policies
questions.e: Per NIST Special Publication 800-14, the three types of security policy are the enterprise information security policy (EISP), the issue-specific security policy (ISSP), and the systems-specific security policy (SysSP).

questions.q: What is the enterprise information security policy (EISP), and how long is it typically?
o: A technical firewall configuration; hundreds of pages

An executive-level document (also called the general or organizational security policy) usually drafted with the CIO, typically 2 to 10 pages long, modified only when the organization's strategic direction changes
A daily operational checklist; one page
A law enforced by the state; variable length
questions.e: The EISP is an executive-level document, usually drafted by or with the organization's chief information officer (CIO); it is typically 2 to 10 pages long and is modified only when there is a change in the strategic direction of the organization.

questions.q: Which type of policy addresses a specific area of technology (such as e-mail or Internet use) and requires frequent updates?
o: Enterprise information security policy (EISP)
Issue-specific security policy (ISSP)
Systems-specific security policy (SysSP)
Constitutional policy
questions.e: The issue-specific security policy (ISSP) addresses specific areas of technology (e.g. e-mail, Internet and Web use, BYOD, portable storage), requires frequent updates, and states the organization's position on a specific issue.

questions.q: Among the three approaches to ISSPs (independent, comprehensive, and modular), which is described as the optimal balance?
o: The independent ISSP
The comprehensive ISSP
The modular ISSP
None of them
questions.e: The modular ISSP is described as the optimal balance between the independent approach (which has a 'scattershot effect') and the single comprehensive approach (which tends to overgeneralize); it is centrally managed but tailored to individual technology issues.

questions.q: What is an access control list (ACL) in the context of systems-specific security policies?
o: A list of all employees in the organization
Details about user access and use permissions and privileges for an organizational asset or resource, focusing on assets and the users who can access them
A list of all network cables
A schedule of policy reviews
questions.e: An access control list (ACL) consists of details about user access and use permissions and privileges for an organizational asset or resource (such as a file storage system or network device); ACLs focus on assets and the users who can access them.

questions.q: How does a capabilities table differ from an ACL?
o: A capabilities table lists cables; an ACL lists users
A capabilities table focuses on users, the assets they can access, and what they can do (also called user profiles), whereas an ACL focuses on assets and who can access them
They are identical
A capabilities table is a law; an ACL is a policy
questions.e: A capabilities table is similar to an ACL but focuses on users, the assets they can access, and what they can do (also called user profiles or user policies); an ACL focuses on assets and the users who can access them. An access control matrix combines both.

questions.q: ACLs regulate access along four dimensions. Which set lists them?
o: Encrypt, hash, sign, and verify
Who can use the system, what authorized users can access, when they can access it, and where they can access it
Confidentiality, integrity, availability, and authenticity
Strategic, tactical, operational, and technical
questions.e: ACLs regulate who can use the system, what authorized users can access, when authorized users can access the system, and where authorized users can access the system.

questions.q: How often should a security policy be reviewed, according to policy management practice?
o: Every ten years
At least annually
Only when it is first written
Never
questions.e: A policy should be reviewed at least annually as part of policy management; this schedule of reviews demonstrates due diligence, and the policy should carry an origin date and revision dates (and may need a sunset clause).

questions.q: What are the five goals (outcomes) of information security governance?
o: Encryption, hashing, signing, auditing, and logging
Strategic alignment, risk management, resource management, performance measurement, and value delivery
Investigation, analysis, design, implementation, and maintenance
Confidentiality, integrity, availability, authenticity, and non-repudiation
questions.e: The five goals/outcomes of information security governance are strategic alignment (of security with business strategy), risk management, resource management, performance measurement, and value delivery.

questions.q: What is the difference between an information security framework and an information security blueprint?
o: A blueprint is a general model; a framework is the customized plan

A framework is a specification of a model to be followed during design and implementation of security controls (a security model), while a blueprint is that framework customized to a specific organization, including implementation details
They are identical
A framework is a law; a blueprint is a policy
questions.e: An information security framework is a specification of a model to be followed during the design, selection, and implementation of all subsequent security controls (also called a security model); a blueprint is a framework customized to a specific organization, including implementation details.

questions.q: The ISO 27002 standard was originally published under which name/number?
o: NIST SP 800-14
British Standard BS7799
FIPS 180-4
The Budapest Convention
questions.e: The model 'Information Technology — Code of Practice for Information Security Management' was originally published as British Standard BS7799; in 2000 it was adopted as ISO/IEC 17799, and it was renamed ISO 27002 in 2007 to align with ISO 27001.

questions.q: How many security control clauses, control objectives, and individual controls does ISO/IEC 27002:2013 contain?
o: 5 clauses, 10 objectives, 20 controls
14 security control clauses, 35 control objectives, and more than 110 individual controls
3 clauses, 5 objectives, 12 controls
27 clauses, 100 objectives, 500 controls
questions.e: ISO/IEC 27002:2013 contains 14 security control clauses, 35 control objectives, and more than 110 individual controls.

questions.q: What is the key difference between ISO 27001 and ISO 27002?
o: ISO 27001 is for certification and setting up an ISMS; ISO 27002 provides implementation guidance and is not used for certification
ISO 27002 is for certification; ISO 27001 is implementation guidance
They are identical
ISO 27001 is a hashing standard; ISO 27002 is a cipher
questions.e: ISO/IEC 27001:2013 explains how to implement 27002 and set up an information security management system (ISMS) and is used as a standard for certification (better as an assessment tool); ISO 27002 provides implementation guidance and is not used for certification.

questions.q: Which three countries refused to adopt ISO/IEC 17799?
o: Pakistan, India, and Bangladesh
The United States, Germany, and Japan
The UK, France, and Italy
China, Russia, and Iran
questions.e: The United States, Germany, and Japan refused to adopt ISO/IEC 17799, citing problems such as its lack of measurement precision, its incompleteness relative to other frameworks, and that it was hurriedly prepared.

questions.q: Which NIST document is titled 'Generally Accepted Principles and Practices for Securing Information Technology Systems'?
questions.e: NIST SP 800-14 is titled 'Generally Accepted Principles and Practices for Securing Information Technology Systems'; SP 800-12 is 'An Introduction to Computer Security: The NIST Handbook'.

questions.q: What is defense in depth?
o: Using a single strong control to protect all assets
A strategy for protecting information assets that uses multiple layers and different types of controls (managerial, operational, and technical) to provide optimal protection
Physically disconnecting systems from networks
Encrypting data twice
questions.e: Defense in depth is a strategy for the protection of information assets that uses multiple layers and different types of controls — managerial, operational, and technical — to provide optimal protection.

questions.q: What are the three types of controls used in defense in depth?
o: Public, private, and hybrid
Managerial, operational, and technical
Strategic, tactical, and operational
Physical, logical, and administrative
questions.e: Defense in depth uses three types of controls: managerial controls (administrative planning and governance/risk management), operational controls (lower-level functionality such as disaster recovery and incident response), and technical controls (firewalls, VPNs, IDPSs).

questions.q: In the 'sphere of use' model of security, what lies at the center as the most important asset?
o: The Internet
Information
People
Networks
questions.e: In the sphere of use, information is at the center as the most important asset; the layers around it, from outer to inner, are Internet, Networks, Systems, People, and Information, with networks and the Internet being indirect threats.

questions.q: The three layers of information security design are commonly referred to by which acronym, and what does it stand for?
o: CIA — Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability
PPT — Policies, People, and Technology
ACL — Access, Control, List
SDLC — Systems Development Life Cycle
questions.e: The three layers of IS design are Policies, People (education, training, and awareness), and Technology, commonly referred to as PPT; policies must be in place before any technical controls can be implemented.

questions.q: The NIST Cybersecurity Framework consists of which five functions?
o: Investigate, Analyze, Design, Implement, Maintain
Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, and Recover
Plan, Do, Check, Act, Review
Disseminate, Review, Comprehend, Comply, Enforce
questions.e: The NIST Cybersecurity Framework's five functions are Identify (what you're protecting), Protect (build safeguards), Detect (install alarms), Respond (have a plan for alarms), and Recover (rebuild after an attack).

questions.q: The 'Big 3' security frameworks are NIST CSF, ISO 27001, and PCI-DSS. Which of these can an organization become certified in and is mandatory for processing credit cards, respectively?
o: NIST for certification; ISO for cards
ISO 27001 is the one you can get certified in; PCI-DSS is mandatory if you want to accept credit cards
PCI-DSS for certification; NIST for cards
All three are optional and none offer certification
questions.e: Among the Big 3 frameworks, ISO 27001's key differentiator is that you can get certified in it, while PCI-DSS (from the Payment Card Industry Security Standards Council) is a non-negotiable, compliance-driven framework you must follow to accept credit cards.

questions.q: What is risk assessment?
o: The application of safeguards to reduce risk
The identification, analysis, and evaluation of risk as the initial parts of risk management
The complete removal of all risk
A hashing operation
questions.e: Risk assessment is the identification, analysis, and evaluation of risk as the initial parts of risk management. Risk treatment (risk control) is the subsequent application of safeguards to reduce risk to an acceptable level.

questions.q: What is risk treatment (risk control)?
o: The identification and analysis of risk
The application of safeguards or controls to reduce the risk to an organization's information to an acceptable level
A calculation of the probability of attack
The removal of an asset from service only
questions.e: Risk treatment (risk control) is the application of safeguards or controls to reduce the risk to an organization's information to an acceptable level.

questions.q: What is risk appetite (risk tolerance)?
o: The total elimination of all risk
The quantity and nature of risk that an organization is willing to accept as it evaluates the trade-offs between perfect security and unlimited accessibility
The probability that a vulnerability will be attacked
The cost of replacing an asset
questions.e: Risk appetite (also known as risk tolerance) defines the quantity and nature of risk that organizations are willing to accept as they evaluate the trade-offs between perfect security and unlimited accessibility.

questions.q: What is residual risk?
o: The risk before any controls are applied
Any remaining risk that has not been removed, shifted, or planned for — the risk left over after the risk management process concludes
The total value of all assets
The probability of a specific attack
questions.e: Residual risk is any remaining risk that has not been removed, shifted, or planned for — the risk that is left over after the risk management process has concluded. The goal is to bring residual risk into line with the risk appetite, not necessarily to zero.

questions.q: In risk management, what is a TVA triple?
o: A three-key encryption scheme
A pairing of an asset with a threat and an identification of the vulnerabilities that exist between the two
A three-phase SDLC
A trio of control strategies
questions.e: A TVA (Threat-Vulnerability-Asset) triple is a pairing of an asset with a threat and an identification of the vulnerabilities that exist between the two, written in a format such as T1V1A2 (Threat 1 to Vulnerability 1 on Asset 2).

questions.q: The five risk control (treatment) strategies are which of the following?
o: Encrypt, hash, sign, audit, and log
Defense, Transference, Mitigation, Acceptance, and Termination
Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, and Recover
Strategic, tactical, operational, technical, and managerial
questions.e: The five risk control strategies are Defense (reduce risk via controls), Transference (shift risk to another party), Mitigation (reduce the impact via contingency planning), Acceptance (accept the current level of risk), and Termination (eliminate risk by removing the asset from service).

questions.q: What does the transference risk-control strategy do?
o: It eliminates the asset from service
It attempts to shift risk to other assets, other processes, or other organizations (e.g. by outsourcing or purchasing insurance)
It reduces the impact of a loss via contingency planning
It accepts the current level of risk
questions.e: The transference strategy attempts to shift risk to other assets, other processes, or other organizations, for example by outsourcing, purchasing insurance, or implementing service contracts.

questions.q: What does the mitigation risk-control strategy rely on, and what are its three contingency plans?
o: Removing the asset; incident, disaster, and business plans
Reducing the impact of a loss through contingency planning: the incident response (IR) plan, the disaster recovery (DR) plan, and the business continuity (BC) plan
Purchasing insurance; three insurance policies
Accepting risk; three acceptance forms
questions.e: The mitigation strategy attempts to reduce the impact of a loss caused by a realized incident through effective contingency planning: the incident response (IR) plan (actions during an incident), the disaster recovery (DR) plan, and the business continuity (BC) plan (the most strategic, involving relocation to an alternate site).

questions.q: Under what condition is the acceptance risk-control strategy a valid choice?
o: When the organization ignores the risk without analysis

Only after determining the level of risk, assessing the probability of attack, estimating potential damage, performing a cost-benefit analysis, and deciding the asset does not justify the cost of protection
Whenever a control is too complex
It is never a valid strategy
questions.e: The acceptance strategy — a conscious decision to do nothing to protect an asset — is valid only after the organization has determined the level of risk, assessed the probability of attack, estimated potential damage, performed a thorough cost-benefit analysis, and decided that the asset does not justify the cost of protection.

questions.q: What is the difference between quantitative and qualitative risk assessment?
o: Quantitative uses ratings like low/medium/high; qualitative uses numbers

Quantitative assigns numeric values (e.g. asset value × likelihood × impact) enabling cost-benefit/ROI analysis, while qualitative uses categories/ratings and expert judgment, is faster and needs less data, but is more subjective
They are identical
Quantitative applies only to hardware; qualitative to software
questions.e: Quantitative risk assessment uses numeric values (such as asset value × likelihood × impact) enabling monetary loss estimates and ROI analysis but requires reliable historical data; qualitative assessment uses categories/ratings (low/medium/high) and expert judgment, is faster and needs less data, but is more subjective.

questions.q: What is likelihood in risk assessment?
o: The value of an information asset
The probability that a specific vulnerability within an organization will be the target of an attack
The number of controls applied
The cost of a disaster recovery plan
questions.e: Likelihood is the probability that a specific vulnerability within an organization will be the target of an attack; if an asset is targeted once every 5 years, its annualized likelihood is 1/5 = 20 percent.

questions.q: A key directive of risk management states that you should never do what?
o: Never apply more than one control
Never spend more to protect an asset than the asset is worth
Never accept any level of risk
Never review a policy
questions.e: A key directive is: never spend more to protect an asset than the asset is worth; this underlies the cost-benefit analysis used in the acceptance strategy.

questions.q: The 'Cardboard Vault' analogy (a titanium lock on a cardboard box left on a sidewalk) illustrates what principle?
o: That physical security is unnecessary
That a strong individual control is worthless without good security architecture — the location and design matter as much as the control
That encryption is the only defense needed
That air gapping always works
