questions.e: The Cardboard Vault analogy shows that a strong control (the titanium lock) on a disastrous architecture (a cardboard box on a sidewalk) provides no real security; it highlights why security architecture — cohesive, multi-layered defense — is paramount.

questions.q: What is 'defense in depth' described as in the security architecture lecture?
o: A single impenetrable wall
An 'onion' approach where multiple layers of security protect assets, so that if one layer is breached, another stands ready — there is no silver bullet in security
The practice of encrypting all data
A physical airlock
questions.e: Defense in depth is described as an 'onion' approach where multiple layers of security protect assets; if one layer is breached, another stands ready. The key lesson is that there is no silver bullet in security.

questions.q: What is a DMZ (demilitarized zone) in network security architecture?
o: A fully trusted internal network
A buffer network between the untrusted (Internet) and trusted (internal) networks — the essence of a screened subnet architecture
A physical airlock for people
A type of firewall rule
questions.e: A DMZ (demilitarized zone) is a buffer network placed between the untrusted network (the Internet) and the trusted internal network — the essence of a screened subnet architecture; if a DMZ server is breached, attackers are still isolated from core assets.

questions.q: Which services are typically placed in the DMZ, versus the internal network?
o: Database servers in the DMZ; web servers internally
Public-facing services (web servers, mail servers, proxy servers) in the DMZ; sensitive assets (database servers, HR records, workstations) in the internal network
Everything is placed in the DMZ
Nothing is placed in the DMZ
questions.e: Public-facing services such as web servers, mail servers, and proxy servers go in the DMZ, while sensitive assets such as database servers, HR records, and employee workstations remain in the internal network, so a DMZ breach keeps attackers far from critical data.

questions.q: In the Target breach example, how did attackers reach the credit card data?
o: They physically stole a server
They exploited a third-party HVAC vendor's credentials to gain network access, then moved laterally to the credit card data — a failure of network segmentation
They cracked the AES encryption
They used a phishing e-mail to the CEO
questions.e: In the Target breach, attackers did not breach the main database directly; they exploited a third-party HVAC vendor's credentials to gain network access and then moved laterally to reach the credit card data, a critical failure of network segmentation.

questions.q: What is air gapping, and which real-world attack shows physical security is information security?
o: Encrypting data at rest; the Target breach
Physically disconnecting critical systems from all networks so the only way to access them is to physically touch them; Stuxnet bypassed air gaps via an infected USB drive
Placing servers in a DMZ; the WannaCry attack
Using a mantrap; the Equifax breach
questions.e: Air gapping means physically disconnecting critical systems (like nuclear centrifuges) from all networks, so the only access is physical. The Stuxnet virus bypassed air gaps, suspected to have been introduced via an infected USB drive, proving that physical security is information security.

questions.q: What is a mantrap in physical security?
o: A software honeypot for catching hackers
A physical airlock requiring multi-factor authentication to access secure areas — the physical equivalent of a proxy server
A type of firewall
A clean-agent fire suppression system
questions.e: A mantrap is a physical airlock requiring multi-factor authentication to access secure areas, ensuring only authorized personnel enter; it is described as the physical equivalent of a proxy server.

questions.q: Why should a data center use a clean-agent fire suppression system (such as FM-200) rather than a standard water sprinkler?
o: Water is more expensive than clean agents
A standard water sprinkler can destroy server hardware, so clean-agent systems suppress fires without damaging electronics, protecting availability (the 'A' in the CIA triad)
Clean agents are required by law
Water sprinklers cannot detect fire
questions.e: A standard water sprinkler system can destroy server hardware; clean-agent systems (like FM-200) suppress fires without damaging electronics, protecting availability — the 'A' in the CIA triad.

questions.q: In the health management system design activity, where should the guest Wi-Fi be placed?
o: On the internal LAN alongside the database
Either completely external or in a highly isolated DMZ segment, never touching the internal LAN
In the same VLAN as employee workstations
Directly on the database server
questions.e: In the secure architecture design, guest Wi-Fi should be either completely external or in a highly isolated DMZ segment, never touching the internal LAN, while the database is deeply protected within the internal network, ideally in a separate VLAN isolated from direct workstation access.

questions.q: What is the difference between the untrusted and trusted networks in security architecture?
o: The untrusted network is the internal LAN; the trusted network is the Internet
The untrusted network is the Internet ('the Wild West'); the trusted network is the internal LAN housing sensitive data
They are the same network
The trusted network has no security controls
questions.e: The untrusted network is the Internet, often called 'the Wild West', while the trusted network is the internal LAN housing sensitive data; a DMZ buffers between them because placing a web server directly in the trusted network would be a huge risk.
